about: The priest spreads his hands over the offerings — a gesture the Roman Mass uses in this one place only — and the server rings the bell: the sign that the consecration is near. The second half of the prayer, from diésque nostros, was added by St Gregory the Great, according to the Liber Pontificalis. The sentence begun back at Communicántes gets its verb only here: quǽsumus, we beseech.

s01.narrative: The priest holds his hands spread over the offerings.

s02.translation: This oblation therefore of our service, and of thy whole household, we beseech thee, O Lord, graciously to accept:

s03.translation: and to dispose our days in thy peace, and bid us be snatched from eternal damnation and numbered in the flock of thine elect.

w001.function: It points at what the priest is at this moment holding his hands over.

w004.function: Servítus is not ordinary service but the condition of a slave; the Canon uses it of a service freely given to God.

w009.function: In Latin a família is a house together with its servants, not the family in our sense; here it is the whole Church.

w011.function: A fossilised parenthesis, like the English “we pray”: it does not govern the sentence but softens it.

w014.function: The adjective agrees with the unstated subject of “accípias” (w015): not be appeased, but receive already appeased.

w016.function: Accusative plural; the -que attached to it joins this clause to the one before.

w026.function: The accusative subject of the infinitive “éripi” (w027): bid that we be snatched away.

w027.function: A passive infinitive depending on “júbeas” (w032), six words further on; the same verb governs “numerári” (w034) as well.

w033.function: An ablative with numerári: numbered within the flock, not added to it.

w036.function: No eúndem here: Christ has not been named in this prayer, so there is nothing to refer back to.
